segments.english: with Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of Goim, Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar: four kings against the five.
segments.literal: with-Chedorlaomer king-of Elam and-Tidal king-of Goim and-Amraphel king-of Shinar and-Arioch king-of Ellasar four kings with-the-five

tokens.note: אֵת here is the preposition 'with' (the pack's lemma is the 'with' entry); it continues the battle report of verse 8
the numeral 'four' with a masculine plural noun takes the feminine form אַרְבָּעָה
the preposition אֵת 'with', as in 14:9.1; of two sides in battle, 'with' means 'against'
definite article on the numeral: the five kings of verse 2

phrases.literal: 'and-Tidal king-of Goim'; each of the later names has ו, which the English gives only before the last
'with the-five'; the second אֵת is again 'with', in the sense of battling against

grammar: The verse is a long apposition continuing verse 8: the four kings are listed with their lands, each as 'king of X', and the list ends with the totals 'four kings against the five'.
אֵת is the preposition 'with' (compare עִם): Ibn Ezra glosses אֵת כְּדָרְלָעֹמֶר as 'with'. It is not the object marker here.

The accents set each name-and-land pair apart: geresh/revia after Elam, pashta/zaqef qaton for the next two pairs, tipha and etnahta at Arioch and Ellasar; the merkha-tipha pair carries 'four kings' and silluq closes 'the five'.
The numerals contrast four against five; the word order 'four kings against the five' sets the few against the many.
segments.note: Both אֵת in the verse (14:9.1, 14:9.16) are the preposition 'with', as the pack parses them and as Ibn Ezra glosses the first (כמו עם); in a battle 'with' the five means 'against' them. Goim (גּוֹיִם) is left as a name, as the lexicon gives it; the word is also 'nations', and Onkelos translates it 'of the peoples' (דְעַמְמִין). Onkelos reads 'Babel' for Shinar.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the few nevertheless won, to show they were mighty, and Abram was not deterred from pursuing them. This is a moral about the numbers, not a reading of the words.
Ibn Ezra glosses אֵת in אֵת כְּדָרְלָעֹמֶר as 'like עִם', that is, 'with'. The English adopts this.

apparatus: Onkelos: 'with Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of the peoples, Amraphel king of Babel, Arioch king of Ellasar, four kings against five.'

segments.english: The Valley of Siddim was pit upon pit of bitumen, and the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled and fell there, and the survivors fled into the hills.
segments.literal: and-valley-of the-Siddim pits-of pits-of bitumen and-fled king-of Sodom and-Gomorrah and-fell-there and-the-remaining to-hill fled

tokens.note: construct state; the verse begins a circumstantial clause with no verb
a place name, with the article
feminine plural construct of בְּאֵר, with the irregular vowels בֶּאֱרֹת; Ibn Ezra notes the change
repeated word expresses plurality: 'pits upon pits'
Rashi and Radak read 'clay, mud' (טִיט), the lexicon 'bitumen, asphalt'
wayyiqtol, plural, with a singular construct subject 'king of'
singular construct serving both names; with the plural verbs the sense is the king of Sodom and the king of Gomorrah (14:2, 14:8), hence 'kings' in the English
שָׁמָּה: שָׁם with the directional he, 'thither', here equal to 'there'
הֶרָה: הַר with directional he, without the article

phrases.english: The Valley of Siddim was pit upon pit of bitumen
phrases.literal: 'and-valley-of the-Siddim pits-of pits-of bitumen'; the doubled noun means many pits

phrases.english: the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled
phrases.literal: 'and-fled king-of Sodom and-Gomorrah'; one construct 'king of' serves both cities, and the plural verb shows two kings
'and-fell thither', that is, into the pits

phrases.english: and the survivors fled into the hills
phrases.literal: 'and-the-remaining to-hill fled'; הֶרָה is indefinite, 'to a hill' (Rashi)

grammar: The doubled בֶּאֱרֹת בֶּאֱרֹת is idiomatic: 'pits and pits', that is, pit after pit. Both words are in the construct state, with חֵמָר 'bitumen' as the last member.
The verb וַיָּנֻסוּ is plural although מֶלֶךְ־סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה looks like a single king 'of Sodom and Gomorrah'. The sense is the king of Sodom and the king of Gomorrah.
הֶרָה and שָׁמָּה take the directional ה, a locative ending without a preposition. Rashi says הֶרָה means 'to a mountain' (indefinite), unlike הָהָרָה with the article, 'to the mountain'.
The word order changes at the end: 'and the remaining ones, to-the-hills they fled', with the subject and place fronted to contrast with the two kings who fell.
Zaqef qaton on חֵמָר ends the first clause; etnahta on שָׁמָּה ends the second.
segments.note: I take חֵמָר as the lexicon gives it ('bitumen'); Rashi and Radak read 'clay, mud' for the building mortar, a reading the English does not adopt. וַיִּפְּלוּ־שָׁמָּה is kept open between 'fell into the pits' and 'threw themselves down there' (Ibn Ezra); the English line says only 'fell there'. הֶרָה is rendered 'into the hills', following Rashi's indefinite reading; Ibn Ezra's 'to the mountain' is recorded. Sforno takes the survivors to be the three remaining kings.

commentary.summary: Rashi: there were many pits there, from which earth was taken for the mortar of buildings. The aggadic midrash: the mud was thick in them, and a miracle was done for the king of Sodom, who came out of it, because some among the nations did not believe that Abraham had been saved from the furnace at Ur Kasdim; once this king came out of the mud, they believed in Abram after the fact. The English takes his 'many pits' but keeps the lexicon's 'bitumen' for the material.

Rashi: הֶרָה is like לְהָר, 'to a mountain', with the ה replacing the לָמֶד at the front; it names no particular mountain, since each fled to whichever he found first, unlike הָהָרָה, which means a known mountain. The English adopts the indefinite reading.

Ibn Ezra: בְּאֵר everywhere in Scripture is a well with flowing water, and its form here (בֶּאֱרֹת) is changed because of the construct. The English accepts the construct, but where he and Rashi differ on the sense it takes Rashi's pits dug for earth rather than wells; his 'wells' is kept here.

Ibn Ezra: וַיִּפְּלוּ שָׁמָּה means they let themselves fall there of their own will, to escape (ברצונם להמלט), as in 'and he fell on his face' (Numbers 16:4). The English keeps the neutral 'fell there', which does not exclude this reading but does not adopt it.
Ibn Ezra: הֶרָה means 'to the mountain' and is a strange word. The English instead follows Rashi's indefinite 'into the hills'; Ibn Ezra's definite reading is kept here.

apparatus: WLC reads הַשִׂדִּים with a different vowel pointing; MAM reads הַשִּׂדִּים (14:10.2).
Onkelos: 'the plain of the field was pits, pits of clay; the king of Sodom and Gomorrah fled and fell there, and those who remained fled to the mountain.'

segments.english: They took all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah and all their food, and went away.
segments.literal: and-took all-of goods-of Sodom and-Gomorrah and all-of their-food and-went

tokens.note: construct state, with a following compound genitive
object marker with ו, a second object
אָכְלָם: 'their food', with the 3rd person masculine plural suffix; the form אָכְלָם is the bound form of אֹכֶל
wayyiqtol of הלך; the entry gives no sense for the plain 'go'

phrases.english: They took all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah

grammar: The verse is a simple chain of wayyiqtol verbs with the plural subject of the four kings.
רְכֻשׁ סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה is a construct chain with a double genitive: 'the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah'.
The repetition of אֶת־כׇּל, 'all', stresses the completeness of the plunder: goods and food.
The telisha gedola on the first word is a prepositive accent, written twice on וַיִּקְחוּ.
segments.note: וַיִּקְחוּ is rendered 'took' with the sense of plundering. Radak says 'their food' includes what was in the houses and the people in them; the English keeps 'food'. The entry for הלך lists no plain-'go' sense in the pack.

commentary.summary: Radak: the Valley of Siddim lay within the border of Sodom and Gomorrah, and the battle was there; Admah, Zeboiim and Bela were not on that side. So the kings took the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah from those cities and their villages, and רְכֻשׁ includes movable property and livestock. The English 'goods' carries this.
Radak: 'their food' means what they had in the houses, 'and the people in them'; the English keeps the plain 'food'.

segments.english: They took Lot, the son of Abram's brother, and his goods, and went away; he was living in Sodom.
segments.literal: and-took [obj] Lot and [obj] goods-his son-of brother-of Abram and-went and-he dwelling in-Sodom

tokens.note: circumstantial clause with a pronoun subject

phrases.literal: 'son-of brother-of Abram'; the phrase is in apposition to Lot
'and-he dwelling in-Sodom'; the participle describes his situation

grammar: וְהוּא יֹשֵׁב is a circumstantial clause: a pronoun plus a participle that states a situation, not a sequence.
בֶּן־אֲחִי אַבְרָם is a double construct chain in apposition to לוֹט, although in the Hebrew it stands after 'and his goods'; the English moves it next to Lot.
The qadma on וַיִּקְחוּ and the darga on לוֹט are conjunctive and lead to the tevir on רְכֻשׁוֹ; the merkha on אֲחִי leads to the tipḥa on אַבְרָם, and the etnaḥta on וַיֵּלֵכוּ ends the first half.
In the second half the merkha on וְהוּא joins the pronoun to its participle, and tipḥa and silluq close the verse: the narrator adds where Lot was living.
segments.note: Ibn Ezra adds that Lot was living in Sodom 'on that day'; the English does not add a 'then'. Rashi's remark that his dwelling in Sodom was the cause is moral and is not a reading of the words.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'Who caused him this? His living in Sodom.' This is a moral comment on the clause, not a reading of its words.
Ibn Ezra: 'he was on that day living in Sodom', which takes the participle as a state of affairs at the time of the capture. The English renders it as a circumstantial clause.

segments.english: The fugitive came and told Abram the Hebrew, who was living by the terebinths of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner; they were allies of Abram.
segments.literal: and-came the-fugitive and-told to-Abram the-Hebrew and-he dwelling in-terebinths-of Mamre the-Amorite brother-of Eshcol and-brother-of Aner and-they masters-of covenant-of Abram

tokens.note: gentilic with the article; Rashi reads it as 'from across the river'
'masters of a covenant': an idiom for those bound by covenant

phrases.english: who was living by the terebinths of Mamre the Amorite
brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner
phrases.literal: 'brother-of Eshcol and-brother-of Aner'; apposition to Mamre

grammar: וְהוּא שֹׁכֵן is a circumstantial clause (pronoun plus participle) about Abram.
'Brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner' stands in apposition to מַמְרֵא; the accents (revia, then mahpakh and pashta) attach it to Mamre, not to Abram.
בַּעֲלֵי בְרִית is an idiom: 'masters of a covenant', that is, allies. The same construction pairs a person with a thing owned.
הַפָּלִיט has the article: 'the fugitive', one particular person known to the story; הָעִבְרִי is its only appearance as a title for Abram.
Etnahta on הָעִבְרִי separates the report from the circumstantial clause that follows.
segments.note: Rashi's plain-sense identification of the fugitive as Og is recorded, not adopted in the English line. הָעִבְרִי is rendered 'the Hebrew'; Rashi's 'from across the river' is a gloss on the name, not an alternative translation. 'Eshcol' has a sense in its entry for a valley; here it is a personal name.

commentary.summary: Rashi: on the plain sense this is Og, who escaped the war (Deuteronomy 3), since Amraphel and his allies did not kill him when they struck the Rephaim at Ashteroth-karnaim. The English says only 'the fugitive'.
Rashi, after Genesis Rabbah: הָעִבְרִי means one who came from across the river. The English keeps 'the Hebrew', which can carry that sense.
Rashi: they had made a covenant with him. The English renders בַּעֲלֵי בְרִית as 'allies'.

Ibn Ezra: הַפָּלִיט is one who fled and escaped, one of the people of Sodom (מבני סדום), as in 'the fugitive from Jerusalem came to me' (Ezekiel 33:21); there is also a midrashic way. The English uses 'the fugitive'.

segments.english: When Abram heard that his brother had been taken captive, he armed his trained men, those born in his household, three hundred and eighteen, and pursued as far as Dan.
segments.literal: and-heard Abram that was-taken-captive his-brother and-armed [obj] his-trained-men born-of his-house eight ten and-three hundreds and-pursued up-to Dan

tokens.note: Lot is Abram's nephew; 'brother' is used of a near kinsman
Hiphil wayyiqtol of רִיק, 'empty out': here to draw out weapons or to equip with them
plural of חָנִיךְ 'trained' with the suffix 'his'; Rashi cites a written form חנכו (singular), which the MAM text does not have
'those born in his house': the household slaves
the numeral 'eight', in a compound with 'ten'
feminine singular of 'three' joined to a plural noun
the pack's sense for עַד is 'until'; here it is local, 'up to'

phrases.english: When Abram heard that his brother had been taken captive
he armed his trained men, those born in his household

phrases.literal: 'eight ten and-three hundreds'; the order is reversed in English

phrases.english: and pursued as far as Dan

grammar: וַיִּשְׁמַע ... כִּי introduces the content of what Abram heard: 'that his brother was taken captive'. The Niphal נִשְׁבָּה is passive.
וַיָּרֶק is Hiphil of רִיק, 'empty out'. The verb is used of drawing a sword (Leviticus 26:33) or a spear (Psalm 35:3), and so here 'armed'; its object is 'his trained men'.

חֲנִיכָיו is the plural of חָנִיךְ with the suffix 'his', from the root חנך, 'train, initiate' (compare 'train up a child', Proverbs 22:6). Rashi cites a singular written form חנכו, which the MAM text does not have.

The number is written 'eight ten and three hundreds': שְׁמֹנָה עָשָׂר 'eighteen' first, then שְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת 'three hundred', with the short form of 'three' because מֵאָה is feminine. English reverses the order.
Etnahta on אָחִיו divides the verse into the news and Abram's response.
segments.note: For וַיָּרֶק I choose 'armed' on the combined view of Rashi (armed, as Onkelos וְזָרִיז) and Ibn Ezra's first reading ('gave them weapons'); his second reading, 'drew out the swords from the sheath', is kept in the commentary entry. Rashi's singular spelling חנכו is recorded in the apparatus. Rashi's midrash that the three hundred and eighteen are Eliezer alone is not adopted, and Rashi's remark on Dan (the later calf-idol) is not a reading of the words.

commentary.summary: Rashi: וַיָּרֶק means 'armed', as Onkelos renders it (וְזָרִיז); so 'I will unsheathe (וַהֲרִיקֹתִי) the sword after you' (Leviticus 26:33) means 'I will arm myself with my sword against you', and so 'I will draw my sword' (Exodus 15:9) and 'draw out the spear and close' (Psalm 35:3). The English takes 'armed'.

Rashi: the word is written חנכו, singular, 'his trained one': this is Eliezer, whom he had trained in the commandments. The word means a person's or a vessel's first entry into the craft it is to serve, as in 'train up a child' (Proverbs 22:6), 'the dedication of the altar' (Numbers 7) and 'the dedication of the house' (Psalm 30). The English renders the plural of the MAM text, 'trained men', in this sense.
Rashi: our rabbis said it was Eliezer alone, which is the numerical value of his name. The English takes the number at face value; the midrash is kept here.
Rashi: there his strength failed, since he saw that his descendants would set up a calf there. This is a homily on the place name, not a reading of the words.

Ibn Ezra: he gave them weapons of war, as in 'and draw out the spear' (Psalm 35:3); some say he drew the sword from its sheath, as in 'they empty their sacks'. The English adopts the first and records the second.
Ibn Ezra: חֲנִיכָיו are those he had trained many times in battle; the gematria of Eliezer is only a homiletic way and the text speaks in its plain sense. The English adopts 'trained men'.

apparatus: Rashi reports the spelling חנכו, singular, 'his trained one', which he reads as Eliezer; the MAM text reads חֲנִיכָיו and the pack records no Ketiv/Qere at this word (14:14.8).

segments.english: He and his servants divided themselves against them by night and struck them, and pursued them as far as Hobah, which is north of Damascus.
segments.literal: and-divided-himself against-them night he and-his-servants and-struck-them and-pursued-them up-to Hobah which from-left to-Damascus

tokens.note: עַל with the suffix, in the sense 'against'
the pronoun 'he' stands after the verb to add the subject
'from the left': the left side when one faces east is the north

phrases.english: He and his servants divided themselves against them by night
phrases.literal: 'and-divided-himself against-them night he and-his-servants'; the verb is singular, then the subject is added, so Rashi reorders to 'he and his servants divided themselves'

phrases.english: and pursued them as far as Hobah

grammar: The singular verb וַיֵּחָלֵק is followed by הוּא וַעֲבָדָיו: the subject 'he and his servants' comes after the verb and the adverb 'by night', which is why Rashi says the verse is transposed.
וַיִּרְדְּפֵם and וַיַּכֵּם have the suffix מ, 'them': the verbs are wayyiqtols and the verb 'pursue' is repeated from verse 14.
מִשְּׂמֹאל לְדַמָּשֶׂק is 'from the left of Damascus' and names the north, taken from the person facing east.
The qadma and darga lead into the tevir on לַיְלָה, which sets 'by night' apart from the pronoun that follows.
segments.note: I follow Rashi's plain-sense reordering: 'he and his servants divided themselves against them by night', as pursuers split up after fugitives who scatter. His aggadic reading, that the night itself was divided in two, is not adopted. For מִשְּׂמֹאל I write 'north of', the sense 3 in the entry. Rashi's remark that no place is called Hobah and that Dan is meant is a midrash and is not adopted; the English keeps the name Hobah.

commentary.summary: Rashi: on the plain sense the verse is transposed: 'he and his servants divided themselves against them at night', as pursuers split into parties after fugitives who flee in different directions. The English adopts this order.

Rashi: 'night' means that even after dark he did not hold back from pursuing them; the English 'by night' follows this plain sense. The aggadic midrash, that the night was divided, with a miracle done for him in its first half while the second half was kept for the midnight of Egypt, is not adopted.
Rashi: no place is named Hobah; Dan is called Hobah because of the idolatry that would be there. This is a homily and the English keeps the name.

segments.english: He brought back all the goods, and also brought back Lot his brother and his goods, and also the women and the people.
segments.literal: and-brought-back [obj] all-of the-goods and-also [obj] Lot his-brother and-his-goods brought-back and-also [obj] the-women and [obj] the-people

tokens.note: Hiphil wayyiqtol with the shortened form וַיָּשֶׁב
the same word as in 14:11, with the article
a perfect verb at the end of its clause

phrases.english: He brought back all the goods
and also brought back Lot his brother and his goods
phrases.literal: 'and-also [obj] Lot his-brother and-his-goods brought-back'; the verb comes last for emphasis

grammar: The first verb, וַיָּשֶׁב, is the Hiphil wayyiqtol of שׁוּב, 'bring back': after the wayyiqtol prefix the long form יָשִׁיב is shortened and its vowel becomes segol. Do not confuse it with וַיֵּשֶׁב 'and he sat, dwelt', from יָשַׁב.
In the second clause the verb is placed last (הֵשִׁיב, perfect), after its double object; this emphasis on Lot sets him apart from the general goods.
וְגַם ... וְגַם ... repeats 'and also' in the verse, as the narrator widens the list from goods to Lot and then to the captives.
The etnaḥta on הָרְכֻשׁ divides the verse in two: the goods, then the persons.
segments.note: הָעָם is rendered 'the people' with the entry sense 4, the persons taken from Sodom. 'Brother' for Lot is as in 14:14.
